name: anandyandawang-plugins
description: Personal Claude Code plugin marketplace. One folder = one plugin.

plugins.name: grug
plugins.description: Talk like grug brain developer. Very clear, very very simple. Fewest words, simple words, short sentences. Brief, high-level — no overexplain. Keeps all technical truth + code exact. Universal: chat, commits, PRs, code comments, reviews.

plugins.name: grug-extremist
plugins.description: grug but EXTREME — applies ONLY to Claude's chat/personality output; commits, PRs, code, comments, reviews and logs stay normal. Hard cap: at most 5-10 words per turn; if the user asks grug to explain, at most 50 words. Brevity beats clarity — short wins even for security/danger/destructive content (grug still says the danger, in few words). Third person 'grug', simple words; code and values stay byte-exact. complexity very very bad. word very bad too.

plugins.name: terse
plugins.description: Hard global cap on output verbosity: at most ~20% of a normal response. Strict, no exceptions. Every medium — chat, commits, PRs, code comments, reviews, logs, docs. Lead with the answer, then stop. Code and technical values stay exact and complete.

plugins.name: codecat
plugins.description: An ASCII-art cat companion that lives in your coding session. It pads in on its own — greets you when a session starts, loafs and does zoomies between turns, celebrates your git commits and pushes, and curls up at session end. Pure art delivered via hooks; never changes how Claude talks. Frequency is tunable.

plugins.name: clear-pr
plugins.description: Write PR titles and descriptions in anandyandawang's house style. Title: a lowercase imperative summary, like a commit subject (no ticket prefix). Body: a single `## Summary` section, 25-100 words (fewer is better), in at least two paragraphs — one on the current state of things ("Currently, …"), one on what this PR does ("This PR introduces …"). As simple, plain and natural English as possible — no fluff — with backticks/code used sparingly, only for particularly important files. Auto-applies when opening a PR; invoke /clear-pr to apply the format on demand.

plugins.name: context-rich-paywithextend-pr
plugins.description: After a PR is created, enrich its description with context a human reviewer wants but the diff can't show. Triggers when a JIRA key (e.g. EX-12345) has been mentioned anywhere in the session: once a PR exists, fetch the ticket via the Atlassian MCP, add a `## JIRA` section linking it, fold the ticket's high-level what/why into the body, and attach Datadog links (traces, logs, metrics, dashboards) where they aid the why. A content enricher, not a formatter — completely independent of clear-pr. Invoke /context-rich-paywithextend-pr to enrich the current PR on demand.

plugins.name: clear-comments
plugins.description: Write code comments in anandyandawang's house style. Comment sparingly — the code says what, a comment says why. Vocabulary is `// TODO:` (with the unblocking condition, and the issue-tracker key in parens when the project uses one) and `// Note:` (an intentional, non-obvious decision); no FIXME/HACK/XXX, no `/* */` block comments, no commented-out code, no restating the line below. Backtick every code identifier. Doc comments are a mini-spec for public interfaces and complex services; inline `//` annotates mapping tables with the source system's label; tests get scenario/section banners. Always-on via hooks — keeps comments sparse and code self-documenting as a persistent default, not just when invoked.

plugins.name: orchestrator
plugins.description: The session's main model is the heaviest, most capable agent available — too valuable to spend punching out lines of code. Orchestration only: plan, decompose, delegate. All implementation goes to cheaper subagents via an explicit model override, picked by role from the current lineup: one tier down is the workhorse carrying nearly all delegated work (coding included, free to orchestrate its own sub-work); the mid tier takes only the simplest tightly-scoped tasks and never orchestrates; the lowest tier goes essentially unused. Never spawn a subagent at the orchestrator's own tier, never omit the override on a coding agent. Afterwards the orchestrator tests and reviews the result itself, then delegates fixes in a small loop until green. Direct edits only when delegating clearly costs more than the change. Always-on via hooks.

plugins.name: plan-big-execute-small
plugins.description: The session's main model is the coordinator: it plans, decomposes, briefs, judges, and synthesizes, but never pulls token-heavy raw material — web pages, long files, log dumps, broad search sweeps — through its own context. Cheap worker subagents with explicit model overrides do that reading in their own parallel context windows and report back distilled findings with evidence and stated uncertainties, so coverage work fans out N-wide and the bulk tokens bill at the cheap rate. Briefs have a floor cost, so bundle related lookups instead of shredding them; small planning peeks and reads where frontier judgment on the raw material is the point stay with the coordinator; untrusted content is read by scoped workers, and current-world facts come from worker reads, not recall. Always-on via hooks.

plugins.name: ultracodinator
plugins.description: Ultracode's standing opt-in, run with right-sized agents. Binds only while ultracode is on for the session; dormant otherwise. The main-loop model is the ultracodinator: it plans phases, authors workflow scripts, writes rich stage prompts, judges results, and synthesizes — and pushes essentially all execution into Workflow orchestrations. Every workflow agent() call and every subagent carries an explicit model override sized to its task — the heaviest model in the lineup is never spawned; it eats tokens like nothing else and exists for coordination alone: the mid tier is the workhorse and default for implementation, design, and verification; the high tier (one below the coordinator) is reserved for the most complex stages; the low tier takes the simplest mechanical stages. Effort overrides follow the same sizing. Never omit the override — omitted means inherit, and inherit means the main-loop model. Direct edits only when orchestrating clearly costs more than the change. Always-on via hooks.

plugins.name: no-comments
plugins.description: Write code with ZERO comments, ever. Never write a code comment of any kind in any language — no `//`, `/* */`, doc comments, docstrings, `#`, `--`, `<!-- -->`, no TODO/Note/FIXME, no commented-out code. The code carries all meaning itself: better names, smaller functions, explicit types, enums, and well-named constants replace every comment. Machine-read directives (shebangs, linter/pragma directives, required license headers) are the only allowed comment-syntax lines. Always-on via hooks. Don't run alongside clear-comments — pick one.
